summary: Specifies a Diameter application for real-time credit control for services such as network access, SIP, messaging, and downloads. It was replaced by RFC 8506.

eli5.summary: Like a prepaid phone card: the system checks you have enough balance as you use the service. A newer document replaced it.

questions: how does credit control work in diameter
how do multiple services share credit in diameter
subtitle: Real-time billing and account management for prepaid services.

tldr.problem: Prepaid services require checking account balance and reserving credit before service delivery, and adjusting the account as the user consumes services. The existing Diameter accounting protocols operate after the fact, not in real-time.
tldr.mechanism: The Diameter Credit-Control application defines a protocol between service elements and credit-control servers. The client requests credit authorization before service delivery, the server reserves funds, the client reports usage periodically, and the server deducts the actual cost. Session state is maintained throughout.
tldr.outcome: Prepaid billing can enforce account limits in real-time across multiple service types (network access, SIP, messaging, downloads). RFC 8506 superseded this with updated requirements.

today: RFC 4006 is a Proposed Standard that has been superseded by RFC 8506, which updates the Diameter credit-control application.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Prepaid services have proven successful in mobile networks, where users buy credit in advance and use services until the credit runs out. As prepaid models expand to wireline networks and IP services, new requirements emerge: checking account balance before service starts, rating service usage in real-time, and adjusting the account as usage occurs. Existing Diameter protocols like NASREQ and DIAMMIP provide authentication and authorization but not real-time credit control. RADIUS Accounting and Diameter accounting protocols report usage after the fact, which is too late for prepaid enforcement.

This RFC specifies a new Diameter application for real-time credit-control. It enables service elements (Network Access Servers, SIP proxies, application servers) to query a credit-control server before granting service, monitor usage during the session, and report the final usage for billing. The system supports prepaid users, advanced features like graceful service termination when credit runs out, and flexible failure handling when the credit-control server is unreachable.
sections.eli5: The system checks if you have enough balance before letting you use the service, watches how much you use, and keeps your account up to date. If you run out of money, it can either kick you off or let you access special services like a top-up portal.

sections.title: Architecture and Components
sections.content:
The credit-control architecture comprises three main entities. The Service Element (NAS, SIP Proxy, or application server) provides the actual service to the end user and hosts the Credit-Control Client, which communicates with the credit-control server. The Credit-Control Server maintains user account information, performs rating (calculating the cost of services), and manages credit reservations. The AAA Server handles authentication and authorization separately; credit-control may interact with it, but operates independently. A Business Support System maintains billing and account databases that the credit-control server accesses.

The credit-control server may exist as a separate logical entity or be combined with the AAA server. Multiple credit-control servers can exist for redundancy and load balancing. The credit-control protocol is the Diameter base protocol with the credit-control application (Auth-Application-Id=4). Service elements communicate with credit-control servers using CCR (Credit-Control-Request) and CCA (Credit-Control-Answer) commands defined by this RFC.
sections.eli5: The service element (like a WiFi router or phone switch) asks the credit server for permission before giving you service. The credit server checks your account and either says yes or no.

sections.title: Credit Authorization Models
sections.content:
The RFC defines two main credit authorization models. In session-based credit-control, the client performs three types of interrogation: initial (before service starts), intermediate (while service is ongoing), and final (when service ends). The server rates the initial request, reserves funds from the account, and returns the quota the client may consume. As the user consumes resources, the client sends intermediate requests reporting usage and requesting more quota. When the session ends, the client sends a final request reporting the last usage, and the server refunds unused reserved credit and deducts the actual consumption.

In one-time event credit-control, the client sends a single request for services like price enquiry, balance check, or direct debiting. The server responds with a single answer; no session state is maintained. This model suits services that do not span time (a one-off download with a quoted price) or administrative operations. The RFC also defines operations for service price enquiry, balance checks, and account refunds.
sections.eli5: For a long activity like a data session, you ask permission first, check in several times as you use data, and settle up at the end. For a quick transaction like buying a ringtone, you ask once and get the answer back.

sections.title: Session Flow and Message Exchange
sections.content:
In session-based credit-control, the client first sends CCR with CC-Request-Type=INITIAL_REQUEST before granting service. It includes the subscription ID, service context ID (identifying the service-specific document), and requested service units (time, volume, or money). The server responds with CCA containing granted service units, validity time (how long the quota lasts), and other control parameters. The client then allows the user to consume up to the granted amount.

Before the granted quota is exhausted or validity time expires, the client sends CCR with CC-Request-Type=UPDATE_REQUEST, reporting used units and requesting new quota. The server deducts the used amount from the account, rates the consumption, reserves new credit, and returns the new quota in CCA. This may repeat multiple times during a long session. When service ends, the client sends CCR with CC-Request-Type=TERMINATION_REQUEST reporting final usage. The server deducts the actual consumption and refunds any reserved but unused credit.
sections.eli5: 1. Client: Can I use 100 MB? Server: Yes, here's 100 MB. 2. Client: I used 80 MB, can I get 100 more? Server: Yes, here's 100 MB more. 3. Client: I used the remaining 20 MB plus 50 of the new 100 MB, I'm done. Server: You owe $2.10, refunding $1.50.

sections.title: Multiple Services and Failure Handling
sections.content:
When multiple services use the same user session (e.g., voice plus messaging), the RFC enables independent credit-control for each service. The client includes the Multiple-Services-Indicator AVP in the initial request; the server responds with separate Granted-Service-Unit values in Multiple-Services-Credit-Control AVPs for each service. Services can be grouped into rating groups (same cost model) or credit pools (shared quota). The client reports usage separately for each service, and the server tracks and deducts independently.

The RFC defines flexible failure handling when the credit-control server becomes unreachable. The client implementation and server policy (via Credit-Control-Failure-Handling and Direct-Debiting-Failure-Handling AVPs) determine whether the client should allow service to continue (accepting risk) or deny service immediately. When credit runs out, the server can send Final-Unit-Indication to tell the client to terminate service, redirect the user to a top-up portal, or restrict access to specific destinations.
sections.eli5: If you're using WiFi and VoIP at the same time, the system tracks credits for each separately so they can cost differently. If the credit server stops working, the local policy says whether you keep going (risky) or get cut off. When you're out of money, the server can kick you off, send you to a payment site, or just block expensive services.
